# breakdown.md
This is a detailed breakdown of every scene in the visual novel,
including locations outfits etc etc.  The actual scenes will be
created using this file as a reference.

---

## How to read this

This breakdown is derived from the five route treatments in `wiki/treatment/`
(Ember, Isolde, Seraphine, Wren, and the dark **Undivided** / polygamy arc) and
the shared act skeleton in `wiki/outline.md`.

**Branch model.** All five routes share one trunk: the opening act and the early
part of act two are the *same* scenes for everyone, coloured only by which love
interest Caedon gravitates toward. The story then forks:

```
COMMON TRUNK (Act I + early Act II)
        │
        ├─ c11_execution  ← the stranded-pair execution beat = the fork
        │
        ├── romance branches (determined by accumulated affection):
        │     ├─ EMBER   (em_*)
        │     ├─ ISOLDE  (is_*)
        │     ├─ SERAPHINE (se_*)
        │     └─ WREN    (wr_*)
        │
        └── DARK BRANCH: "The Undivided" (ud_*)
              — taken when Caedon has committed to NO single love interest;
                it diverges AT c11_execution and never rejoins.
```

The four romance branches reuse every trunk scene verbatim; they differ only in
their act-two tail and act three, and each ends in a wedding. The dark branch is
foreshadowed from Act I by *how* Caedon plays the trunk (cataloguing rather than
courting), but only formally splits off at the execution beat, and ends in
conquest + a timeskip civil war, no wedding.

are stable handles for the eventual `[[scene: ...]]` markers and

A nineteen-year-old scholarship student at the Cog-College of Cograuncy, born to a Ferran furnace-town family of modest means. Caedon is lean and wiry from years hauling coke on the furnace floors, with dark tousled hair, storm-grey eyes, and a smear of engine soot that never quite washes out from under his nails. He carries himself with a watchful, self-taught steadiness — the wariness of someone who has always been the outsider in a room of guild-born peers.

Unusually, Caedon draws on both Currents — a faint pull of ordered Sela and wild Vash alike — a rarity the College has not yet decided whether to prize or fear. He channels without a Governor by instinct, which terrifies his professors and thrills the Kiln-Sworn recruiters. Earnest, stubborn, and quick to defend those the guild-state overlooks, he is the still point around whom the other students orbit.

A Kiln-Sworn forge-prodigy from the Vashan Dominion, Ember is Vash-strong and channels raw, ungoverned current with a reckless brilliance that terrifies her instructors. Broad-shouldered and sun-dark, with close-cropped copper hair and the first faint rust-scarring already tracing her right forearm — a mark she wears like a dare. She grew up in Cinderhold's forge-quarters, tending engine-fires before she could read, and came to the Cog-College half as a prodigy and half as a Dominion test of whether their heresy could be tamed by Ferran licensing. It cannot. Hot-tempered, loyal, and allergic to caution, she believes power is meant to be spent, not metered — and privately fears how little time the Rust will leave her. Beneath the swagger is someone who loves fiercely because she does not expect to love long.

Raised where the Assayers hold sway and channeling is tightly leashed, she was taught to distrust the Weave even as it woke strong in her — Sela-strong, precise and cold as her homeland. She wears her piety like armor and her doubt like a hidden knife: the more she sees of ungoverned power, the harder her convictions are tested. Grey silk, iron clasps, a single key-shaped pendant. Beneath the frost is a young woman aching to be more than her province's leash.

Raised in the soot-warrens beneath Cograuncy, she is a fugitive by birth: her mother was severed by the Assayers, and Wren has spent her life one filed-smooth cog-token ahead of the Grey Hands. She smuggles the hunted through the cloudlanes and trades in forbidden weaves. Sharp, wary, and fiercely loyal to the discarded, she hides a raw Vash strength she can no longer safely hold. Her hands bear the first faint bloom of Rust-scarring, which she keeps gloved. Beneath the guardedness is a starved hunger to be trusted by someone who won't sell her.

Gideon Marsh is a broad-shouldered, steady-handed Cog-College student from the Saltbound Crownland, the son of a harbor-city shipwright. Where others chase power, Gideon chases competence: he is the group's anchor, slow to anger and impossible to rattle. Sela-strong in the Stone Thread, he favors structural weaves — bracing, binding, mending — and dreams of building airship keels rather than fighting. He wears his Governor without complaint and thinks the Concord's rules are mostly sensible, which puts him at odds with the hotter heads around him. Loyal to a fault, he is the friend who carries the wounded and pays the tab. Broad face, sun-weathered from a childhood on the docks, close-cropped brown hair, and forearms scarred from foundry work.

The youngest and smallest of the friend-circle, Pip Calloway is a wiry Amberline street-orphan turned Cog-College scholarship prodigy. Where others channel, Pip tinkers — a gearsmith and Governor-hacker whose nimble fingers can coax a regulator into doing things its makers never licensed. He talks fast, filches faster, and has an informant in every workshop and kitchen from the boiler-decks to the deans' tower. Barely a channeler at all — a flicker of Sela, no more — he compensates with cleverness and cheek, and a loyalty to his friends fiercer than his slight frame suggests. Amberline taught him that knowing everyone's secrets is the only reliable currency, and he collects them like a magpie collects brass.

Ferran-born to a family of furnace-engineers, he is Sela-strong and Concord-trained, more comfortable with a Governor bolted to his forearm than without it. Practical, loyal, and slow to anger, he is the anchor of the friend group — the one who reads the manual, checks the pressure gauges, and hauls everyone out of trouble. Headmistress of the Cog-College, a woman in her late fifties who wears authority like a well-oiled mechanism. Auria rose through the Regulen Concord as a Sela-strong administrator rather than a battle-channeler, and she runs the College the way the Ferran Ascendancy likes its institutions run: metered, licensed, and accountable. Silver hair coiled tight beneath a brass circlet, a high slate-and-white coat of office, and a Governor gauntlet she rarely needs but always wears as a symbol. She is shrewd, fair, and quietly political — she must keep Concord inspectors, Dominion recruiters, and half a dozen monarchies' heirs all under one roof without the place burning down. Beneath the protocol is genuine care for her students and an old, private doubt about what the Assayers do with those the College severs.

Professor Mirabel Quist is the Cog-College's mistress of Governors — the artificer-scholar who teaches the theory and craft of the brass-and-crystal regulators that meter a channeler's flow. A wiry woman in her fifties with cropped iron-grey hair, ink-stained fingers, and a jeweler's loupe forever pushed up on her forehead, she moves through her workshop amid a clutter of half-built gauntlets, crystal blanks, and pressure gauges. Sela-strong and Concord-trained, she believes fervently that measured power is the only safe power, yet she is no dogmatist: she quietly studies the failures of Governors, including the ones the Concord would rather bury. Warm, blunt, and endlessly curious, she treats students as apprentices and machines as puzzles. She is the professor most likely to notice when a student's talent outruns their Governor — and the one who understands exactly how dangerous that is.

A gaunt, severe man in his late fifties, Professor Silas Thorn teaches the theory and discipline of Governors at the Cog-College — the brass-and-crystal regulators that meter a channeler's flow. Ferran to the bone and a devoted man of the Regulen Concord, he believes utterly that only measured power is safe power, and he drills that creed into every student who passes through his laboratory. His long fingers are stained with crystal-etching acid and his forearm bears a licensed Governor he has never once removed in public. Thorn is exacting, cold, and quietly brilliant; he has forgotten more about the mechanics of the Weave than most channelers ever learn. Beneath the rigor is an old grief — a former student who burned out under his instruction — that he has sealed away behind procedure. He distrusts the Kiln-Sworn as heretics and the Ashen Circle as criminals, and he watches any student who leans toward raw Vash with the wariness of a man who has seen where it ends.

# Treatment — Ember Kellan Route

Expanded story treatment for the route where Caedon's primary love interest is **Ember Kellan**, the Kiln-Sworn forge-prodigy of the Vashan Dominion. The throughline is raw, ungoverned Vash power set against Ferran licensing — and the slow shadow of the Rust that will one day take her. It is a romance lived under a sentence: Ember loves fiercely because she does not expect to love long, and the tragedy of the route is Caedon's refusal to accept that verdict.

## Act One — The Spark

Caedon arrives at the Cog-College among a licensed, metered intake and is immediately drawn to the one student who refuses to be measured. Ember Kellan channels raw current in the practice yards where the cautious hang back — copper-haired, broad-shouldered, her right forearm already tracing the first bloom of rust-scarring, which she bares rather than hides. Her reckless brilliance both alarms and magnetizes him.

He learns her position: she is the Vashan Dominion's test case, a Kiln-Sworn heresy the Ferran licensers mean either to tame or to make an example of. She resents both her keepers and the collar. Among the other male students Caedon finds his footing; with Ember he finds a live wire.

In class, Caedon watches Ember chafe against metered channeling — she can do the disciplined thing and refuses to, believing power is meant to be spent, not hoarded. He begins to see the rust-scarring not as damage but as a dare she throws at the world.

The friend group is sent to investigate ruins as part of a test. When nefarious external actors intervene, Ember spends power without counting the cost, saving the group but burning herself doing it. They emerge victorious. In the aftermath Caedon sees, for the first time, the true price of her recklessness — and that she paid it gladly for them.

# Treatment — Isolde Vorn Route

**Logline.** A devout daughter of the Grey Principality, sent south to spy as much as to study, discovers that the order she was raised to trust is the rot behind the world's collapse — and that the ungoverned talent she was taught to fear is the only thing worth believing in.

**Central conflict.** Doubt against devotion. Isolde's cold Sela precision is inseparable from the piety that leashes it; Caedon's route is the slow, painful unclasping of that armor until she chooses her own thread.

## Act One — The Watcher

Caedon arrives at the Cog-College among licensed talents and is drawn to Isolde Vorn: an aristocrat's stillness, a devout's certainty, and a wit sharp enough to cut through both. She keeps him at arm's length — a Vorn daughter does not befriend ungoverned talent lightly, and she is here to watch as much as to learn.

In class, Caedon sees how tightly Isolde leashes her own Weave, and how her convictions flinch whenever power is used freely. Her key-pendant marks her as more than a student.

The friend-group ruins test goes wrong when nefarious actors intervene. Isolde's disciplined, precise weaving saves them where recklessness would have failed — but winning forces her to break a rule she genuinely believes in, and the transgression shakes her to the core.

Caedon is pulled into the conflict around her: Vorn's watchers, the Assayers' long reach, and the open question of whether Isolde is a student or a spy.

# Treatment — Seraphine Halcyon route

The diplomat's path. Where the outline sketches the beats, this treatment expands them into a scene-level throughline. The spine is Seraphine's struggle between the peace-broker role her mother groomed her for and her hunger to choose her own thread — and the slow discovery that the courts she was raised to trust are complicit in the war for who controls the Weave.

## Act one — The watched daughter

Caedon arrives at the Cog-College among a cohort of licensed talents and finds Seraphine Halcyon at the center of every room without seeming to seek it: silver-blonde, unhurried, cloud-grey eyes that miss nothing. She is surrounded by Loomwright-inclined peers and a rotating attendance of envoys who treat a student as a piece on a board. Caedon is charmed past her practiced court reserve precisely because he wants nothing from her house — a novelty she does not know what to do with.

In class he watches her braid Spirit and Air with a delicacy that unnerves the instructors, who are used to force, not thread. He glimpses the peace-broker future her mother has arranged and the quiet resentment beneath her grace. Their early scenes trade in wit and indirection; she tests whether he is another courtier and finds, to her unease, that he is not.

The friend group is sent to investigate the ruins as a test. When nefarious actors intervene, it is Seraphine's perceptiveness that reads the ambush and her diplomacy that turns a losing fight — talking, misdirecting, and weaving where the others would have swung. They emerge victorious, but she alone recognizes the intervention as no accident: someone with reach arranged it. Caedon is drawn into the tangle around her — rival houses courting Halcyon Reach, a treaty whose fine print hides who truly means to leash the Weave.

# Treatment — Wren Ashfield Route

A story of trust extended to someone who has never been able to afford it. Wren Ashfield is a burned-out channeler and cloudlane smuggler of the Ashen Circle underground; the emotional engine of the route is whether she can believe Caedon will not sell her, and whether he can prove worthy of a loyalty that has only ever cost her.

## Act One — The Outsider

Caedon arrives at the Cog-College a half-step out of place: a talent without the polish of the licensed houses. Among the intake he keeps colliding with Wren, a scholarship outsider who moves through the College's rules as if they were weather to be slipped, not obeyed. She is quick-eyed, guarded, and openly contemptuous of anyone official-looking — she assumes they will hand her to the Grey Hands the moment it profits them.

In class Caedon sees the machinery of punishment up close: ungoverned channeling is a crime, and the College trains its students partly to police it. Wren sits with her Rust-scarred hands gloved and hidden, answering nothing she isn't forced to. Caedon notices, and — crucially — says nothing, keeps her secret without being asked. This is the first coin of trust.

The friend group is sent to investigate a set of ruins as a field test. The 'nefarious external actors' who intervene turn out not to be rival students but Grey Hand Assayers hunting a fugitive channeler who fled into the same ruins. The test becomes a real escape. Wren's smuggling contacts — a cloudlane cache, a bolt-hole — are the only reason the group gets out alive. They emerge victorious, but Wren's cover is torn: she has used the Circle's resources in front of witnesses, and the Assayers now have her scent.

Caedon is drawn fully into the conflict that surrounds her: the Assayers' hunt for severed and unlicensed channelers, and the Ashen Circle that smuggles the discarded to safety.
